name: Pectoralis major rupture
summary: A rupture of the pectoralis major, usually the tendon avulsing from the humerus in a strong man during a heavy bench press or a forced tackle. It causes chest and axillary bruising, a lost axillary fold and weak adduction.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: After repair, return to resisted training about 9 weeks and to full sport commonly 3 to 6 months (case reports and a case series; clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean 11.1 weeks to competition after repair in 20 Australian Football League players; one footballer returned to full contact at 87 days and a wrestler to competition at 24 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Loss of the anterior axillary fold and chest contour with resisted horizontal adduction; no accuracy figures were found for clinical tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI is used to confirm the site and extent of tear and tendon retraction; ultrasound is an alternative (accuracy figures not found)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Men aged 20 to 40 years; mean 26.5 years in elite Australian footballers

keyFacts.label: Strength after surgery versus none
keyFacts.value: Peak torque 99% of the uninjured side after repair versus 56% without repair in one small retrospective comparison

overview:
Pectoralis major rupture is an avulsion of the pectoralis major tendon from its humeral insertion, most often during a heavy bench press or a forceful abduction or hyperextension of the arm. Ruptures are increasing in incidence because of greater awareness, participation by young men aged 20 to 40 years, and anabolic steroid use, and many chronic ruptures go unrecognised [r1]. Weightlifting or bench pressing is the most common mechanism [r2]. In 16 injuries with video footage in elite Australian Football League players, three mechanisms were identified: horizontal hyperextension (62.5%), hyperflexion with abduction (25.0%) and horizontal adduction in a sustained tackle (12.5%), and the sternocostal head insertion was torn in 91.0% [r3]. A tear from parachute static line entanglement also occurs, and in that mechanism 40% of patients had a concomitant injury, most often involving the biceps brachii [r4].

The operative versus non-operative evidence consists of small retrospective comparisons and case series, with low-quality evidence overall. In a retrospective comparison of 22 complete distal tears, peak torque was 99% of the uninjured side after surgical repair (10 tears) and 56% without it (12 tears), and patients who had surgery had better functional outcomes [r5]. In 17 cases (13 repaired, 4 managed non-operatively), the subjective ratings were 96% for acute repair, 93% for chronic repair and 51% without surgery, and isokinetic adduction strength was 102%, 94% and 71% (tested in only eight patients, two of them non-operative) [r6]. A review concluded that non-operatively managed patients lose strength but regain full range of motion, and that non-operative care is indicated in older patients, those with medical comorbidities, incomplete tears or irreparable damage [r1]. On timing, the evidence conflicts. The review reported that repair before 6 weeks gave better outcomes than repair at 6 to 8 weeks [r1], but a systematic review and meta-analysis of 259 cases found no statistical difference in outcomes between acute repair and repair more than 8 weeks after injury, and it rated the evidence as low quality [r7].

Most reports are of young, athletic men who chose or were advised to have surgery, so the comparison with non-operative care is confounded. Repair is usually recommended for active people. Return to sport takes months, and strength deficits and fear of re-injury can persist: in 12 military service members repaired at a mean of 471 days after injury, bench press one-repetition maximum was 19.04% lower and 58.3% were afraid to bench press at their previous weight [r8].

epidemiology.text: Pectoralis major rupture is relatively rare but increasing, with a rise attributed to greater awareness, activity among young males aged 20 to 40 years, and anabolic steroid use [r1]. Weightlifting or bench pressing is the commonest mechanism, and most patients are men aged 20 to 40 years [r2]. In elite Australian footballers, 22 pectoralis major injuries were recorded over 20 years (about 1.1 per year), at a mean age of 26.5 years (range 21–32) [r3]. In a series of 17 distal ruptures, the mean age at injury was 29 years and 10 of 17 injuries were from weightlifting [r6]. The injury is also seen in military personnel, in whom parachuting static-line entanglement is an additional mechanism [r4]. No population incidence rate was found in the sources reviewed.

intrinsic: Male sex and age 20 to 40 years [r1,r2]
Anabolic steroid use, cited as a contributor to the rising incidence [r1]
Muscle hypertrophy and heavy training load (clinical observation)
Previous pectoral or tendon injury (clinical observation)
extrinsic: Heavy bench press and other eccentric chest loading [r1,r2]
Contact and grappling sports, including tackling and being pulled into horizontal hyperextension [r3]
Static-line parachuting and other traction events [r4]
Poor technique or maximal loading without a spotter (clinical observation)

mechanism.summary: The classic description is a forceful eccentric contraction of the pectoralis major while the arm is abducted, extended and externally rotated (textbook description). Weightlifting and the bench press are the commonest mechanism overall [r2], and in filmed AFL injuries the commonest mechanism was horizontal hyperextension [r3]. The load exceeds the tensile strength of the tendon-bone junction, and the tendon, most often the sternocostal head, avulses from the humerus [r3]. A forced traction injury can produce a similar tear [r4].
sequence: The athlete lowers or is driven into a position of horizontal hyperextension or abduction with the arm externally rotated, which lengthens the pectoralis major to its end range [r3].
The muscle contracts eccentrically against a maximal load (a heavy bench press) or against a tackler or opponent, so the tendon takes a very high tensile force [r2,r3].
The sternocostal head tendon is most stretched, and its fibres fail at or near the humeral insertion, producing an avulsion [r3].
The tear may extend through the tendon to include the clavicular head; the tendon retracts medially and the muscle belly retracts (a 5 cm retraction on MRI was reported in one footballer) [r9].
Blood tracks into the chest wall, axilla and upper arm, producing ecchymosis, and the anterior axillary fold is lost.
The patient feels a sudden tear and pain, and adduction and internal rotation strength falls.

variants.name: Bench press or weightlifting avulsion
variants.description: The most common mechanism in the sources reviewed; occurs in men aged 20 to 40 years, sometimes with anabolic steroid use [r1,r2].

variants.name: Horizontal hyperextension in contact sport
variants.description: The most common mechanism in 16 filmed AFL injuries (62.5%), with the sternocostal head insertion torn in 91.0% [r3].

variants.name: Horizontal adduction in a sustained tackle
Traction injury (parachute static-line entanglement)
variants.description: Associated with a concomitant injury in 40% of cases, most often to the biceps brachii [r4].

variants.name: Musculotendinous junction or muscle belly tear
variants.description: Less common than tendon avulsion; may be incomplete and managed non-operatively (clinical convention).

anatomy.text: The pectoralis major is a broad, fan-shaped muscle with a clavicular head from the medial clavicle and a larger sternocostal head from the sternum and upper costal cartilages (and the abdominal head from the rectus sheath). The tendon is a flat, bilaminar structure that inserts on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove of the humerus. The muscle adducts, internally rotates and horizontally adducts the arm, and its lower sternocostal fibres are the most stretched when the arm is abducted and extended. The lower border of the muscle forms the anterior axillary fold. In the AFL series the sternocostal head insertion was torn in 91.0% of injuries [r3]. The biceps tendon runs in the groove just beneath the insertion, which is why associated biceps injuries have been reported with traction mechanisms [r4].

structures.name: Sternocostal head and tendon
structures.role: Main adductor and internal rotator; its humeral insertion is the usual site of avulsion (91.0% of AFL injuries) [r3]

structures.name: Clavicular head
structures.role: Flexion and horizontal adduction; may be spared in partial tears

structures.name: Pectoralis major tendon insertion on the humerus (lateral lip of the bicipital groove)
structures.role: The tendon-bone junction where most ruptures occur [r3]

structures.name: Anterior axillary fold
structures.role: Contour formed by the lower border of the muscle; lost after rupture

structures.name: Long head of biceps tendon
structures.role: Lies in the groove next to the insertion; concomitant injury was most often to the biceps in a parachute-injury series [r4]

structures.name: Anterior deltoid and subscapularis
structures.role: Neighbouring structures that can be injured with traction mechanisms [r4]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In most reported pectoralis major ruptures the tendon fails at its insertion on the humerus (an avulsion), with the sternocostal head affected in 91.0% of injuries in one series [r3]. It occurs when a high eccentric force exceeds the strength of the tendon-bone junction, often in a young, strong muscle, and anabolic steroid use has been linked to the rising incidence [r1]. After a complete tear the tendon retracts (5 cm on MRI in a footballer) [r9], and the muscle belly shortens and bunches toward the chest.

Untreated, complete ruptures cause lasting deformity and weakness. The review reports that patients managed non-operatively lose strength but regain full range of motion, and that chronic tears (over 8 weeks) are more likely to need reconstruction with an autograft or allograft [r1]. In a small comparison, peak torque was only 56% of the uninjured side after non-operative care, compared with 99% after surgical repair [r5].

structures.name: Pectoralis major tendon (humeral insertion)
structures.effect: Avulsion, usually of the sternocostal head; complete tears retract [r3,r9]

structures.name: Pectoralis major muscle belly and MTJ
structures.effect: Haematoma and retraction; muscle belly tears are less common (clinical convention)

structures.name: Biceps brachii and its long head tendon
structures.effect: Concomitant injury in 40% of parachute static-line tears, most commonly the biceps [r4]

structures.name: Anterior deltoid and subscapularis
structures.effect: Partial tears have been reported with traction mechanisms [r4]

structures.name: Skin and subcutaneous tissue
structures.effect: Ecchymosis across the chest, axilla and arm and loss of the axillary fold (clinical observation); ecchymosis and loss of shoulder contour were documented in a case report [r2]

muscles.name: Pectoralis major
muscles.effect: Pain-related inhibition, then real weakness in horizontal adduction and internal rotation; peak torque 56% of the uninjured side without repair in one small study [r5]

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid and biceps
muscles.effect: Compensate in forward flexion and pressing; may be involved in the same injury [r4]

muscles.name: Pectoralis minor and serratus anterior
muscles.effect: Altered scapular control and protraction with weakness (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi and posterior shoulder muscles
muscles.effect: Unopposed pull can increase posterior dominance and altered posture (clinical observation)

cellular.description: Bleeding from the torn tendon and muscle tracks into the chest wall and arm; neutrophils and macrophages clear debris.

Fibroblasts and new capillaries lay down disorganised collagen. If the tendon is repaired, tendon-to-bone healing at the footprint is slow and weak at this stage, which is why the repair is protected.
Collagen is replaced by aligned type I fibres along the lines of load; return to resisted training in case reports began at about 9 weeks [r10].
The tendon scars and shortens, making primary repair harder; reconstruction with graft is then more likely [r1].

systems.effect: Acute nociceptive pain with a tearing sensation; pain-related inhibition of adduction; fear of movement and re-injury [r8]
Extensive ecchymosis across the chest, axilla and arm; large haematoma is possible but expanding or tense swelling needs review
Anabolic steroid use is cited as a contributor to the rising incidence of ruptures; ask about it respectfully [r1]
Altered scapular position, posture and pressing mechanics; the opposite shoulder and trunk may compensate (clinical observation)
In 12 repaired military patients, 58.3% were afraid to bench press at their previous weight because of fear of re-injury [r8]

grading.system: Descriptive classification by tear location and completeness (no single universally accepted system)

grades.description: Part of the tendon or muscle torn, with some residual function. Non-operative care is indicated for incomplete tears [r1].
grades.prognosis: Usually functional with rehabilitation; monitor for progression (clinical convention).

grades.grade: Complete tendon avulsion from the humerus
grades.description: The commonest pattern in the sources reviewed; the sternocostal head insertion was torn in 91.0% of AFL injuries [r3].
grades.prognosis: Repair is generally recommended for active people; surgery gave better strength and function than non-operative care in small retrospective comparisons [r5,r6].

grades.grade: Musculotendinous junction or muscle belly tear
grades.description: Less common; may be managed non-operatively unless complete (clinical convention).
grades.prognosis: Generally better prognosis for non-operative care than avulsion (clinical convention); evidence is limited.

grades.description: Acute repair is usually within the first weeks; chronic ruptures (over 8 weeks) are more likely to need graft reconstruction [r1].
grades.prognosis: Outcomes after repair did not differ statistically between acute and chronic repair in a meta-analysis of low-quality evidence [r7] and a small series [r6], although a review reported better results before 6 weeks than at 6 to 8 weeks [r1].

timeframes.summary: The sources reviewed here are small series and case reports, so the time course below is indicative. After repair, resisted training began at about 9 weeks and sport-specific drills at 14 weeks in a wrestler [r10]; a footballer returned to full contact at 87 days [r9]; and the mean return to competition was 11.1 weeks in AFL players [r3].

healing.description: Sling and passive or protected motion within the surgeon's limits; no resisted pectoral loading.
Progress active range, scapular control and then light resisted work. In case reports resistance training began about week 9 [r10].
Progressive horizontal adduction and pressing strength, then sport-specific drills (week 14 in one wrestler) [r10].
Return to full contact at 87 days in a footballer [r9]; competition at week 24 in a wrestler [r10]; mean 11.1 weeks in AFL players [r3].

milestones.label: Surgery (acute repair)
milestones.note: 75% of AFL repairs within 1 week of injury [r3]

milestones.label: Resistance training begins after repair
milestones.note: Week 9 in one wrestler [r10]; follow the surgeon's protocol

milestones.label: Mean return to competition in AFL players after repair
Full contact training in a professional footballer
Return to competition in a world-class wrestler

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not time-based. Reported times after repair range from about 11 weeks (AFL mean, range 8–15 weeks) [r3] to 87 days to full contact [r9] and 24 weeks to competition in a wrestler [r10], and these were elite athletes with a structured program. For recreational lifters, commonly 4 to 6 months before a maximal bench press (clinical convention). Return to maximal pressing is limited by strength and by fear of re-injury [r8].

symptoms: A sudden tearing sensation or pop in the chest, axilla or upper arm during a heavy lift or forced arm movement
Immediate pain at the front of the shoulder and chest, with weakness of pressing and adduction
Bruising that spreads over the chest wall, axilla and upper arm within hours to days (clinical observation)
A change in chest shape, with a bulge or hollow at the front of the shoulder
Difficulty with push-ups, pressing, throwing and carrying
Pain on lying on the affected side and reaching across the body
signs: Ecchymosis and loss of shoulder contour with bulking over the chest, as documented in a case report [r2]; bruising commonly extends across the chest wall, axilla and arm (clinical observation)
Loss of the anterior axillary fold, with asymmetry of the chest contour on resisted adduction (clinical observation)
Bulging of the retracted muscle belly toward the chest and a visible hollow in the axillary region
A palpable defect or absent tendon at the humeral insertion
Weak horizontal adduction and internal rotation compared with the other side [r5]
Tenderness along the muscle and tendon, with swelling in the first days

subjective: Mechanism: bench press (load, position, phase), grappling or tackle, parachute or other traction event [r2,r3,r4]
A pop or tearing sensation and the immediate effect on strength
Anabolic steroid or other drug use, asked about without judgement [r1]
Prior shoulder, chest or biceps injuries and previous training load
Hand dominance, occupation, sport, training goals and expectations about surgery
Time since injury, because chronic ruptures change the options [r1]
observation: Ecchymosis across the chest, axilla and arm
Chest contour and the anterior axillary fold, at rest and with the hands pressed together in front of the chest
Muscle retraction or bulging, comparing both sides with the arms at the sides and abducted
Swelling and any associated biceps contour change (concomitant injury) [r4]
palpation: Palpate along the muscle from the sternum and clavicle to the humeral insertion for a gap or thickening
The tendon at the humeral insertion (lateral lip of the bicipital groove) for tenderness or absence
The biceps muscle belly and long head tendon for concomitant injury [r4]
The anterior deltoid, AC joint and sternoclavicular joint
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive shoulder range in all planes; range is usually preserved apart from pain
Horizontal abduction and external rotation (painful stretch of the torn muscle)
Cervical and thoracic spine screen if pain does not fit
strength: Resisted horizontal adduction and internal rotation, compared with the other side
Resisted forward flexion, external rotation and abduction for the cuff
Hand-held dynamometry when available; strength loss without repair was marked in small studies [r5,r6]
neuro: Brachial plexus and peripheral nerve screen after high-energy mechanisms
Distal pulses, capillary refill and sensation if swelling is marked
Cervical screen if symptoms are unclear
functional: Grappling or contact tolerance for athletes
Work tasks that need pushing and lifting

specialTests.name: Observation of the axillary fold with resisted horizontal adduction
specialTests.purpose: To detect loss of pectoralis major continuity
specialTests.procedure: With the shoulders abducted to about 90° and the hands pressed together in front of the chest, or with resisted adduction, compare the muscle contour and anterior axillary fold on both sides.
specialTests.positive: Loss or webbing of the axillary fold, retraction of the muscle belly or a bulge. Accuracy figures were not found in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Palpation of the tendon and the humeral insertion
specialTests.purpose: To locate the tear and identify a defect
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the tendon from the muscle belly to the humeral insertion and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: A defect, absent tendon or point tenderness at the insertion. Accuracy figures were not found.

specialTests.name: Resisted horizontal adduction and internal rotation strength test
specialTests.purpose: To identify strength loss and compare function
specialTests.procedure: Test with the arm at 90° of flexion or at the side, comparing with the other side, preferably with a dynamometer.
specialTests.positive: Marked weakness or pain with a visible contour change. Strength after non-operative care was 56% and 71% of the uninjured side in two small studies [r5,r6], but these are not diagnostic accuracy figures.

clinicalRules.name: A bench press injury with bruising and a lost fold is a rupture until proven otherwise
clinicalRules.description: Many chronic ruptures are unrecognised, and the patient may present late [r1]. Refer for imaging and an orthopaedic opinion early, because the options narrow after about 8 weeks [r1], although some data show no difference between acute and later repair [r7].

clinicalRules.name: Look for concomitant injury with traction mechanisms
clinicalRules.description: In parachute static-line tears, 40% of patients had a concomitant injury, most often to the biceps brachii or anterior deltoid [r4].

clinicalRules.name: Do not rely on one test
clinicalRules.description: No accuracy figures for clinical tests were found in the sources reviewed here; diagnosis rests on the mechanism, bruising, contour change, strength loss and imaging [r2,r9].

outcomeMeasures.name: Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE)
outcomeMeasures.use: Reported after repair in military service members (mean 80.8) [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score
Isokinetic or hand-held dynamometry for horizontal adduction and internal rotation
outcomeMeasures.use: Peak torque and work compared with the uninjured side [r5,r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: One-repetition maximum bench press
outcomeMeasures.use: Reported as 19.04% lower after repair in one series [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Force-plate isometric testing (Athletic Shoulder test)
outcomeMeasures.use: Maximal and rapid force production in one wrestler [r10]

imaging.indication: Suspected rupture, to confirm the site and extent, and for surgical planning
imaging.findings: Complete rupture of the tendon and its retraction (5 cm retraction in one footballer; complete tear of the sternal head in another case) [r9,r2]

imaging.indication: Acute or chronic rupture when MRI is unavailable or to assess the muscle and tendon dynamically
imaging.findings: Tendon gap and haematoma (clinical convention; accuracy figures not found in the sources reviewed)

imaging.indication: After trauma, to exclude fracture or dislocation
imaging.findings: No tendon information; may show avulsion fragment (clinical convention)

differentials.name: Proximal (long head) biceps rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Popeye deformity of the arm and anterior shoulder pain; can coexist with pectoralis major injury after traction mechanisms [r4].

differentials.name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
differentials.distinguishing: Weakness of elevation and external rotation with lag signs after a fall or pull; chest and axillary bruising is not typical.

differentials.name: Anterior shoulder dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Loss of the round shoulder contour and fixed external rotation until reduced; may coexist with muscle tears.

differentials.name: Proximal humerus fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness, crepitus and extensive bruising after a fall; confirmed on radiograph.

differentials.name: Pectoralis major muscle strain or contusion
differentials.distinguishing: Muscle-belly pain and bruising with intact tendon and contour; strength less affected and function recovers with rehabilitation (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Rib fracture or costochondral injury
differentials.distinguishing: Pain on deep breathing and focal rib tenderness without loss of the axillary fold.

differentials.name: Costochondritis
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the costochondral junctions, no history of acute trauma and no bruising.

differentials.name: Acute cardiac event or other chest cause
differentials.distinguishing: Chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or radiation to the jaw or arm; needs emergency assessment rather than a musculoskeletal explanation.

redFlags: Chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or pain radiating to the jaw or left arm after exertion: possible cardiac cause. Emergency assessment before attributing to a muscle injury.
A complete tear in an active person: refer for MRI or ultrasound and an orthopaedic opinion early, because chronic ruptures (over 8 weeks) are more likely to need reconstruction with a graft [r1].
Rapidly expanding swelling, tense arm or axilla, or a cold, pale or numb hand: possible significant haematoma or vascular injury. Emergency assessment.
High-energy or traction mechanism (parachute static line, motor vehicle, fall from height): look for concomitant biceps, deltoid, subscapularis or bony injury [r4].
Fever, a hot red swollen wound or drainage after surgery: possible infection. Same-day medical review.

After repair: a sudden pop, new bulge or loss of strength during rehabilitation suggests re-rupture (one of 20 repaired AFL players re-ruptured within 4 weeks) [r3]. Contact the surgeon and stop loading until reviewed.
Anabolic steroid use with other possible complications (cardiac, endocrine or liver effects): raise it respectfully and refer for medical review when relevant [r1].

management.principles: Diagnose early, because the options narrow with time. Complete tendon avulsions in active people are usually repaired. In small retrospective comparisons, surgical repair restored peak torque to 99% of the uninjured side versus 56% without it [r5], and subjective ratings were 96% (acute repair), 93% (chronic repair) and 51% (non-operative) [r6]. A review recommends non-operative care for older patients, those with comorbidities, incomplete tears or irreparable damage, and notes that patients managed non-operatively lose strength but regain full range of motion [r1]. All the comparative evidence is low quality: retrospective, small, with selection bias, and the systematic review of surgical technique was rated level 4 with low-quality evidence [r7]. Be open about this when counselling. Rehabilitation, with or without surgery, is progressive and criteria-based, and the physiotherapist should address fear of re-injury as well as strength [r8].

medical.name: Early imaging and orthopaedic referral
medical.description: Refer a suspected complete tear for MRI or ultrasound and an orthopaedic opinion promptly, because many chronic ruptures go unrecognised [r1] and chronic tears (over 8 weeks) are more likely to need graft reconstruction [r1]. Early diagnosis keeps the options open even though some data show similar outcomes with later repair [r7].

medical.name: Surgical repair of a complete tendon avulsion in an active person
medical.description: In a retrospective comparison of 22 complete distal tears, peak torque was 99% of the uninjured side after repair versus 56% without it [r5]. In 17 cases, subjective ratings were 96% after acute repair and 93% after chronic repair versus 51% without surgery, and adduction strength 102%, 94% and 71% [r6]. In elite AFL players, 91.0% had repair, 75% within a week, with a mean 11.1 weeks to return to competition and a 5.0% re-rupture rate [r3]. All the data are retrospective, from small series with selection bias; the systematic review rated the evidence as low quality [r7].

medical.name: Timing of repair (acute versus delayed)
medical.description: A review reported that surgery before 6 weeks gave better outcomes than surgery at 6 to 8 weeks, and that chronic ruptures (over 8 weeks) are more likely to need reconstruction [r1]. In contrast, a meta-analysis of 259 cases found no statistically significant difference in outcomes between acute repair and repair more than 8 weeks after injury [r7], and a small series found no significant difference between acute (under 2 weeks) and chronic repair [r6]. The evidence conflicts and is of low quality.

medical.name: Fixation technique
medical.description: In a meta-analysis of 265 cases, the odds of an excellent or good outcome were higher for transosseous suture (odds ratio 6.28, 95% CI 1.37–28.75) and for suture anchor (odds ratio 3.40, 95% CI 1.06–10.85) than for unicortical button, but one study may have skewed the button result; all three techniques were considered acceptable options, and the technique should be the one the surgeon is most proficient in [r7]. Intramedullary suture anchors were used in military service members (mean SANE 80.8) [r8].

medical.name: Non-operative management
medical.description: Indicated for older patients, medical comorbidities, incomplete tears or irreparable damage [r1]. Patients lose strength but regain full range of motion [r1]. In small series, peak torque was 56% of the uninjured side and adduction strength 71% without repair [r5,r6]. Accept the strength loss only after an informed discussion, particularly for heavy lifters and athletes.

medical.name: Chronic rupture: reconstruction with graft or tendon transfer
medical.description: Chronic ruptures (over 8 weeks) increase the likelihood of reconstruction with autograft or allograft; delayed repair had significantly better strength, satisfaction and outcomes than non-operative treatment in the review, and tendon transfer has unpredictable outcomes but overall satisfactory results [r1]. In 12 military service members repaired a mean of 471 days after injury, 83% were extremely satisfied, but bench press one-repetition maximum was 19.04% lower [r8].

physio.name: Education, protection and early symptom management
physio.description: Explain the injury and the options, protect the arm in a sling if surgery is planned, control pain and keep the elbow, wrist and hand moving. Screen for concomitant injuries and cardiac causes, and take a respectful history of any anabolic steroid use [r1,r4].

physio.name: Progressive criteria-based rehabilitation after repair
physio.description: Protected motion first, then active range, scapular control, light resisted work and progressive pressing and adduction strength, following the surgeon's protocol. In reported cases, resistance training began at week 9 and wrestling-specific drills at week 14 in a wrestler [r10], and a footballer returned to full contact at 87 days after tests including hand-held dynamometry, the closed kinetic chain upper extremity test and progressive falling activities [r9]. These are single case reports, not trials.

physio.name: Objective strength monitoring and return-to-sport testing
physio.description: Compare peak and rapid force with the other side using dynamometry or force plate. In one wrestler, net peak force symmetry improved by week 11 but rate of force development at 200 ms lagged behind peak force, so peak strength alone may miss deficits [r10]. This is a single case report.

physio.name: Addressing fear of re-injury and graded exposure to pressing
physio.description: In 12 repaired military service members, 58.3% were afraid to bench press at their previous weight, and the authors suggested that reduced strength may reflect fear rather than physiological limits [r8]. Progress loading in clear steps, with education and shared goals.

physio.name: Treating a missed rupture as a simple muscle strain without imaging
physio.description: Many chronic ruptures go unrecognised, and the options narrow after about 8 weeks [r1]. A bench press injury with bruising and loss of the axillary fold should be imaged and referred early.

physio.name: Early resisted pressing, horizontal abduction stretching or maximal bench press after repair
physio.description: Loading the repair too early risks re-rupture, which occurred in one of 20 repaired AFL players within 4 weeks of surgery [r3]. Follow the surgeon's protocol and use objective criteria, not time alone.

education: A pectoralis major tear is a tear of the tendon where the chest muscle attaches to the upper arm. Heavy bench pressing and forceful pulling or tackling are the usual causes.
Get the injury assessed early. Bruising across the chest and arm, a pop and a change in chest shape are signs of a tear, and the options are best explained soon after injury.

Surgery is usually advised for active people with a complete tear. People managed without surgery usually keep full range of motion but lose strength, which may matter if you lift heavy or play contact sport [r1,r5].
After surgery, the repair needs time to heal. Resisted training usually starts around two months, and return to sport takes several months [r10,r3].
It is common to feel nervous about heavy pressing after a repair. Gradual, measured progression helps to restore confidence [r8].
Seek urgent help for chest pain or breathlessness, a rapidly swelling arm, a cold or numb hand, fever or a sudden loss of strength after surgery.

rehab.overview: The program below is for rehabilitation after surgical repair, with modifications for non-operative care. No trial of rehabilitation after pectoralis major rupture was found in the sources reviewed; the staging is based on case reports [r10,r9] and clinical convention, and the surgeon's protocol takes priority. Progression is criteria-based. Doses are clinical conventions, not trial-derived prescriptions.

stages.name: Protect and restore passive motion
goals: Maintain elbow, wrist and hand function
Begin gentle passive motion within the surgeon's limits
precautions: No resisted adduction, internal rotation or pressing
Avoid horizontal abduction, extension and combined abduction with external rotation beyond the surgeon's limits
No lifting, pushing or pulling with the arm
Report a pop, new bulge, swelling or numbness

exercises.name: Pendulum swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang and swing from the trunk

exercises.name: Elbow, wrist and hand range of motion and grip
Supine passive elevation within limits
exercises.cues: Relax the shoulder; stop at the first firm resistance or the surgeon's limit

exercises.name: Scapular setting and posture
exercises.cues: Gently draw the shoulder blades back and down; avoid shrugging

progressionCriteria: Passive range within the surgeon's targets
Surgeon's clearance to start active motion

stages.name: Active motion and early loading
goals: Begin light resisted work when cleared (resistance training began at about week 9 in a wrestler) [r10]
precautions: No heavy pressing or resisted horizontal adduction until cleared
Avoid loaded end-range horizontal abduction or extension
Keep pain ≤ 3–4/10 during exercise, settling within 24 hours (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Active elevation in the scapular plane
Wall slide
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blade moving; stop short of pain

exercises.name: Isometric internal rotation and light adduction at the side (when cleared)
exercises.cues: Press into a wall with the elbow bent; build over days

exercises.name: Band row
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down; do not stretch into horizontal abduction

progressionCriteria: Full or near-full active range without pain

stages.name: Progressive strengthening
goals: Restore horizontal adduction, internal rotation and pressing strength
Reintroduce loaded pressing in a controlled way
precautions: Increase load by about 5–10% per week and monitor pain over the next 24 hours (clinical convention)
Avoid loaded end-range horizontal abduction, such as deep dips or fly stretches, until cleared

exercises.name: Incline or wall push-up plus
exercises.cues: Push through the hands and protract at the top

exercises.name: Band or cable chest press, limited range
exercises.cues: Slow lowering; stop before the end of horizontal abduction

exercises.name: Band external and internal rotation at the side
Dumbbell row
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Prone Y raise
exercises.cues: Lift with the lower trapezius, not the neck

progressionCriteria: Strength about 80% or more of the other side for horizontal adduction and internal rotation
Pain ≤ 2/10 with loaded pressing and daily tasks

stages.name: Return to heavy pressing and sport
stages.timeframe: Months 4–6 (clinical convention; elite athletes were faster in case reports) [r3,r9,r10]
goals: Restore full strength and rapid force production
Return to bench press, push-ups and contact
precautions: Return to maximal bench press and contact only when criteria are met
Build load in clear steps; fear of re-injury is common [r8]

exercises.name: Barbell or dumbbell bench press, progressive loading
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 6–10 at 7–8/10 effort, 2 times per week, progressing over 8–12 weeks
exercises.cues: Controlled lowering with a spotter; elbows about 45–60° from the trunk (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Push-up progression
exercises.cues: Straight trunk; protract at the top

exercises.name: Explosive horizontal pressing and medicine ball throws
exercises.cues: Fast concentric, soft catch; quality first

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills (tackling, grappling, falling progressions)
exercises.dosage: Start at about 25–30% of normal volume and build over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first, then volume, then contact

progressionCriteria: Passes strength, range and function criteria (see return to sport)
Completes sport simulation at full intensity with pain ≤ 2/10

criteria: Surgeon clearance after repair, with attention to the fixation and time from surgery
Pain ≤ 2/10 with pressing and sport tasks and no night pain
Full or near-full range of motion equal to the other side
Horizontal adduction and internal rotation strength about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
Rate of force development at or near the other side, not only peak force [r10]
Progression to bench press and push-up at a load the athlete is confident to use, with fear of re-injury addressed [r8]
Completes sport-specific training, including contact and falling progressions, without symptoms [r9]
tests: Hand-held dynamometry or isokinetic testing for horizontal adduction and internal rotation [r5,r6]
Force-plate isometric testing in several shoulder angles, including rate of force development [r10]
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test [r9]
Bench press or push-up repetition maximum progression [r8]
Progressive falling and contact activities for contact athletes [r9]

prognosis: Outcomes after repair are generally good in the available series, but the evidence is low quality. In elite AFL players, 91.0% were repaired, the mean return to competition was 11.1 weeks, and 5.0% re-ruptured (one player, within 4 weeks of surgery) [r3]. In a comparison of 22 tears, peak torque was 99% of the uninjured side after repair versus 56% without surgery [r5], and in 17 cases the subjective ratings were 96% (acute repair), 93% (chronic repair) and 51% (non-operative) [r6]. A review concluded that patients treated with delayed repair had significantly better strength, satisfaction and outcomes than patients treated non-operatively [r1]. Residual deficits are common: in military service members repaired at a mean of 471 days after injury, bench press one-repetition maximum was 19.04% lower, 83% were extremely satisfied, and 58.3% were afraid to bench press at their previous weight [r8]. Most of this evidence comes from small retrospective series and case reports in young male athletes, so outcomes in women, older adults and non-athletes are less certain.
prevention: Use sound bench press technique and a spotter, and avoid maximal loading in the bottom range with the elbows far from the trunk (reasonable principle; not tested in the sources reviewed)
Build load progressively and keep a balanced program for the chest, scapular and posterior shoulder muscles (reasonable principle)
Discuss the risks of anabolic steroids, which have been linked to the rising incidence of ruptures [r1]
Teach tackling and grappling technique that avoids forced horizontal hyperextension, the most common mechanism in AFL injuries [r3]
Report acute chest or axillary pain after a lift or tackle early, rather than training through it [r1]
clinicalPearls: Bruising across the chest and axilla, a lost axillary fold and sudden weakness after a heavy bench press or a forced tackle is a pectoralis major rupture until proven otherwise [r2,r3].
In AFL players the commonest mechanism was horizontal hyperextension (62.5%), not only the bench press, and the sternocostal head insertion was torn in 91.0% [r3].

The comparison of surgery with non-operative care is small and retrospective: peak torque 99% versus 56% [r5] and adduction strength 102% versus 71% [r6]. Tell patients that the data are low quality but consistent in direction.

The evidence on timing conflicts: repair before 6 weeks was better than at 6 to 8 weeks in a review [r1], but a meta-analysis of 259 cases and a small series found no significant difference between acute and later repair [r7,r6]. Refer early, but do not tell someone who presents late that nothing can be done.
Measure rate of force development as well as peak strength before return to sport: in a wrestler, peak force symmetry returned by week 11 but 200 ms force lagged [r10].
Address fear of pressing: 58.3% of repaired military patients were afraid to bench at their previous weight, and the strength deficit may partly reflect fear [r8].

animation.title: How a pectoralis major rupture happens

forces.label: Heavy load on the lengthened pectoral

captions.text: A lifter bench presses a heavy bar with the elbows out from the trunk.
He lowers the bar under control: the pectoralis major works eccentrically.
At the bottom, the arm is extended and abducted, and the muscle is at its longest.
The tendon fails at the humerus with a sudden tear, and the bar drops.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.
The pectoralis major tendon inserts on the humerus, beside the bicipital groove.
A heavy eccentric load with the arm abducted and extended stretches the tendon.
The tendon avulses from the humerus, most often the sternocostal head.
The muscle retracts toward the chest, and the axillary fold is lost.
Blood tracks into the chest wall and arm, and the lifter notices bruising and weakness.
Healthy tendon: aligned, crimped type I collagen with a few resident tenocytes.
Under load the crimp straightens and the fibres stretch.
A very high eccentric force exceeds the strength of the tendon-bone junction.
Fibres rupture, leaving a gap with frayed, retracted ends.
Torn vessels bleed into the gap and the surrounding muscle.
Inflammation: neutrophils and macrophages clear debris.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised collagen. After repair, tendon-to-bone healing is slow and the repair is protected.
Remodelling is slow, which is why resisted training waits for weeks to months.
